exercises.name: Unison Drone
exercises.details: Match the held note exactly and blend into it. When you're in tune, the wobble in the sound disappears. Keep it steady as you change the vowel.

exercises.name: Octave Over a Drone
exercises.details: Leap up to the same note an octave higher and let it lock with the drone. It should feel like the same note, only lighter.

exercises.name: Fifth Over a Drone
exercises.details: The fifth is the most stable interval after the octave. Listen for the moment it locks in with the drone and sounds smooth and full.

exercises.name: Fourth Over a Drone
exercises.details: The fourth sounds open but a little unsettled over the drone. Hold it steady without drifting toward the notes next to it.

exercises.name: Third Over a Drone
exercises.details: The major third gives the drone a warm, sweet color. Listen for the moment your note blends in instead of buzzing against it.

exercises.name: Sixth Over a Drone
exercises.details: The sixth is a wide but sweet interval. Hear it in your head before you leap, so it lands in tune instead of being reached for.

exercises.name: Seconds Over a Drone
exercises.details: Seconds rub against the drone and want to move. Hold them steady anyway, then let each one settle back onto the drone's note.

exercises.name: Scale Over a Drone
exercises.details: Some notes rest easily on the drone and others pull away from it. Feel which ones want to move, and tune each one against the drone.

exercises.name: Minor Scale Over a Drone
exercises.details: The third, sixth and seventh notes sit lower than in the major scale and give the drone a darker color. Tune them carefully on the way up and down.

exercises.name: Major Chord Tones
exercises.details: The chord holds still while you sing through its notes. Every note you sing is already in the chord, so listen for it and blend in.

exercises.name: Minor Chord Tones
exercises.details: The same idea in minor. The middle note is lower and darker, so find it inside the chord before you sing it.

exercises.name: Major or Minor
exercises.details: The chord has no third, so your note decides its mood. Sing the bright major third first, then the darker minor third a semitone lower.

exercises.name: Changing Chord Tones
exercises.details: The chord changes every four beats and you sing through the notes of each one. Notice which notes stay and which ones move.

exercises.name: Common Tone
exercises.details: Your note stays the same while the chords change around it. Notice how it feels different in each chord, and keep it exactly in tune.

exercises.name: Third Below
exercises.details: You sing a simple line while another voice moves a third above you. Listen to both at once and don't drift up to the other voice.

exercises.name: Third Above
exercises.details: The melody is played below you and you sing a third above it, the most common harmony part in pop and folk songs.

exercises.name: Sixth Below
exercises.details: The other voice sings a sixth above you as you walk down the scale. Sixths sound full and sweet, so let your voices blend.

exercises.name: Parallel Fifths
exercises.details: This hollow, ancient sound comes from medieval chant. Sing a fifth below the melody and keep the interval pure and steady.

exercises.name: Contrary Motion
exercises.details: You walk down the scale while the other voice walks up, and you cross in the middle. Keep your own direction and don't follow theirs.

exercises.name: Scale Canon
exercises.details: The played voice sings the same scale two beats behind you. Keep going at your own pace and don't let the echo pull you back.

exercises.name: Pedal Point
exercises.details: You are the low note that stays put while the chords above you move. Keep it grounded and steady, even when it clashes with them.

exercises.name: Complete the Chord
exercises.details: Each chord is missing one note, and you sing it. Listen to the notes you're given and fill the gap so the chord sounds complete.

exercises.name: Cadence Top Part
exercises.details: Sing the top part of a simple three-part cadence. Only your first note is played, so hold your line against the other two parts.

exercises.name: Cadence Bottom Part
exercises.details: Now sing the lowest of the three parts. Your line barely moves, so keep it solid and in tune while the parts above you change.

exercises.name: Cadence Middle Part
exercises.details: The middle part is the hardest to hold, with voices above and below you. Listen to both and find your place between them.

exercises.name: Pop Progression Top Part
exercises.details: Sing the top part over the four chords behind countless pop songs. Only your first note is played, so lock your line into each chord.

exercises.name: Pop Progression Bottom Part
exercises.details: The lowest of the three parts moves down a step and comes back. Keep it steady and let the chords change around you.

exercises.name: Pop Progression Middle Part
exercises.details: The inner part moves the most in this progression. Listen to the parts above and below you and keep yours clear between them.

exercises.name: Harmony Below a Tune
exercises.details: Sing the lower part of a short duet. Your line mostly follows the tune a third below, so keep listening to it without slipping onto it.

exercises.name: Harmony Above a Tune
exercises.details: Now you sing the upper part. Stay a third above the tune and keep your voice light, so the melody can still be heard underneath.

exercises.name: Suspended Fourths
exercises.details: Your note starts as a clash inside the chord and then falls a step to settle. Lean into the clash, then resolve it cleanly.

exercises.name: Suspended Seconds
exercises.details: This time your note starts a step below where it wants to be and rises to settle. Keep the clash steady before you move up.

exercises.name: Dominant Seventh Chord Tones
exercises.details: This four-note chord wants to resolve somewhere. Sing through its notes and listen for the top one, which rubs against the bottom.

exercises.name: Major Seventh Chord Tones
exercises.details: A soft, dreamy chord heard in jazz and pop ballads. The seventh sits a semitone below the top note, so keep the two clearly apart.

exercises.name: Minor Seventh Chord Tones
exercises.details: A mellow chord at the heart of jazz and soul. Keep each note relaxed and let it melt into the chord.

exercises.name: Diminished Chord Tones
exercises.details: Every step in this tense chord is a minor third. Keep the steps small and even, so the chord doesn't drift out of shape.

exercises.name: Seventh Resolution
exercises.details: Your note stays put while the chord changes under it and turns it into a clash. Hold it, then let it fall a step to resolve.

exercises.name: Leading Tones
exercises.details: Twice your note is pulled up a semitone into the next chord. Let each leading tone lean upward and land right in the center of the next note.

exercises.name: Chromatic Common Tone
exercises.details: The chords shift into unexpected keys while your note stays put. Hold it steady and listen to how each new chord colors it.

exercises.name: Minor Cadence Top Part
exercises.details: Sing the top part of a minor cadence. The note before the last is only a semitone below the final note, so let it lean upward into it.

exercises.name: Minor Cadence Bottom Part
exercises.details: The lowest part steps up, then drops below where it started and rises a semitone to finish. Tune that last step carefully against the chord.

exercises.name: Minor Cadence Middle Part
exercises.details: The middle part rises a semitone and comes back while the other parts move around it. Hold your place between them.

exercises.name: Counterpoint Above
exercises.details: Your line moves against a slow played melody, in the style of Renaissance counterpoint. Let each interval ring before you move on.

exercises.name: Counterpoint Below
exercises.details: Now the slow melody is above you and you sing the lower voice. Keep your notes grounded and listen to the space between the two voices.

exercises.name: Guide Tones High
exercises.details: These are the notes that define each chord in a jazz progression. Your note holds over the first change and then slips down a semitone.

exercises.name: Guide Tones Low
exercises.details: The other guide tone line through the same progression. Your note slips down a semitone on the first change and then holds.

exercises.name: Blues Third
exercises.details: The blue note sits between minor and major. Touch the lower third quickly and lift into the major third over the bluesy chord underneath.

exercises.name: Barbershop Circle
exercises.details: Each chord leads into the next around the circle of fifths, in barbershop style. Your line moves down by semitones, so make every step small and exact.
